core: Definition of media literacy as the ability to access, analyze, evaluate, create, and act using all forms of communication (NAMLE)
Core concepts: construction; media languages with codes and conventions; differing audience experiences; commercial and ideological interests; values and points of view
Analytic questions to ask of any media text: creator, purpose, audience, techniques, omissions, and differing interpretations
Why media literacy matters: participation, citizenship, and resilience against mis- and disinformation
Skepticism versus cynicism as the analytical stance of media literacy
supporting: Media literacy as a skill set distinct from media criticism and from specialized topics such as advertising, news, and propaganda
Media literacy education as the field dedicated to teaching the skills
Media literacy as not an anti-media movement
outOfScope: Propaganda and its specific techniques (own topic: film-and-media-studies:foundations:propaganda)
News media institutions and practices (own topic: film-and-media-studies:foundations:news-media)

claims.claim: Media literacy is defined as the ability to access, analyze, evaluate, create, and act using all forms of communication.

A central premise of media literacy education is that all media messages are constructed; analysis treats messages as built from choices about selection, arrangement, and technique rather than as transparent reflections of reality.

Each medium communicates through its own language: unique codes, conventions, and constructions; in moving images these include shots, editing, camera movement, lighting, and sound, which together form a shared cinematic language.

Different people experience the same media message differently; individuals construct personal meanings from their own skills, beliefs, and experiences, so interpretation is not identical across audiences.
Media institutions function as commercial entities, media experiences are shaped by systems of power, and all media messages contain values and points of view.
Media literacy education teaches learners to ask questions about the substance, source, form, and significance of media experiences, including whose perspectives are represented or omitted.

Media literacy education aims to develop informed, reflective, engaged, and socially responsible participants in a democratic society and promotes interest in news and current events as a dimension of citizenship.

UNESCO frames media and information literacy as essential skills for engaging critically with information and navigating online environments safely, and as a response to the proliferation of mis- and disinformation, hate speech, and declining trust in media.
NAMLE describes the stance of media literacy education as skeptical rather than cynical and states that media literacy is not an anti-media movement.
Media analysis in media literacy education is evidence-based, open-ended exploration rather than a search for single predetermined correct interpretations.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Terminology: NAMLE defines 'media literacy' with the access/analyze/evaluate/create/act formulation, while UNESCO uses the broader term 'Media and Information Literacy' (MIL), centered on information competencies and the digital environment.
positions: NAMLE: media literacy is the ability to access, analyze, evaluate, create, and act using all forms of communication.
UNESCO: media and information literacy covers critical engagement with information, safe navigation of online environments, and trust in the information ecosystem, including digital competencies.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson adopts NAMLE's definition as the primary framing and cites UNESCO only for the civic and resilience rationale, without equating the two terms.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The classic 'five core concepts' are widely attributed to the Center for Media Literacy (with the fifth concept phrased as messages organized to gain profit and/or power), while NAMLE's Core Principles express the same ideas through principles on construction, media language, audience meaning-making, commercial media institutions, and values/points of view.
positions: Center for Media Literacy list of five core concepts (profit and/or power framing).

NAMLE Core Principles: messages constructed (2.1, 4.1); media language codes and conventions (4.2); personal meaning construction (2.2); media institutions as commercial entities and systems of power (7, 9); messages contain values and points of view (7.2).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the five ideas in NAMLE's framing and cites NAMLE's Core Principles directly. The CML page was unreachable during research (connection timeouts), so its exact list was not reproduced.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The six key questions in the lesson (who created this, for what purpose, for whom, with what techniques, what is omitted, how do others see it differently) are a synthesis; NAMLE's Core Principles support asking questions about substance, source, form, and significance (7.1) and about represented or omitted perspectives, but NAMLE does not publish this exact six-question list on the pages consulted.
positions: A single canonical published list of key questions exists in some frameworks (e.g., the Center for Media Literacy's five key questions).
NAMLE's Core Principles emphasize question-asking (4.3) and analysis of substance, source, form, and significance (7.1).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the six questions as a practical checklist that grows out of the field's core principles, supported by NAMLE's question-asking principles, and never attributes the exact list to a specific organization.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained no substantive factual claims; its boilerplate (media literacy as 'a foundational concept in Film & Media Studies' and a concept students use to 'organize information') carried no verifiable content and was discarded.
The draft's circular vocabulary definitions (e.g., 'Media Literacy: A foundational Film & Media Studies concept covered in this lesson') were replaced with source-verified definitions.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the boilerplate draft with a definition anchored to NAMLE's published formulation (access, analyze, evaluate, create, act).

Added the five core concepts, each verified against NAMLE's Core Principles (construction; media language; differing audience experiences; commercial and ideological interests; values and points of view).
Added an evidence-based six-question analytic checklist for any media text.
Added the skeptical-not-cynical distinction from NAMLE Core Principle 7.4 and the not-anti-media statement from NAMLE's Media Literacy Defined page.
Replaced circular vocabulary definitions with non-circular, source-consistent definitions.
Replaced all generic examples with original invented scenarios (transit film, renovation video, product video).
rightsIssues: No source prose is reproduced; all examples are original and invented.
NAMLE Core Principles page states its works are CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; the University of Arkansas open textbook chapter is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. Both cited with attribution (ATTRIBUTION_REQUIRED).
No license statement was found on NAMLE's Media Literacy Defined page or the UNESCO page; both are classified REFERENCE_ONLY and no license is claimed for them.

sourceRecords.title: Core Principles of Media Literacy Education
sourceRecords.provider: National Association for Media Literacy Education (NAMLE)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live at namle.net (fetched 2026-08-21). Provides the definition of media literacy (access, analyze, evaluate, create, act using all forms of communication); principles 2.1 and 4.1 (all messages/experiences are constructed), 4.2 (each medium has unique language codes and conventions), 2.2 and 3.4 (individuals construct personal meanings; different perspectives), 7.1 and 7.2 (media experiences have perspective, context, purpose; messages contain values and points of view), 7 (media institutions as cultural institutions and commercial entities), 9 (systems of power), 7.4 (skeptical not cynical), 10 (informed, reflective, engaged, socially responsible participants in a democratic society; citizenship). The page states its works are licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. Used as reference; the lesson is original synthesis.

sourceRecords.title: Media Literacy Defined
sourceRecords.provider: National Association for Media Literacy Education (NAMLE)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live at namle.net (fetched 2026-08-21). Confirms the five-verb definition; describes media literacy as empowering people to be critical thinkers and makers, effective communicators, and active citizens; describes media literacy education as the field dedicated to teaching the skills; states media literacy is not an anti-media movement. No license statement found on the page; used as reference only, no wording adapted.

sourceRecords.title: Media and Information Literacy
sourceRecords.notes: Read live at unesco.org (fetched 2026-08-21). Supports the rationale: media and information literacy enables people to engage critically with information and navigate the online environment safely, helps build trust in the information ecosystem, and addresses the proliferation of mis- and disinformation, hate speech, and declining trust in media; frames informed, critical, and engaged citizens as the goal. UNESCO's term is 'Media and Information Literacy'; cited for the rationale only. No license statement verified on the page; used as reference only.

sourceRecords.title: How to Watch a Movie (Moving Pictures, Chapter 2)
sourceRecords.provider: University of Arkansas Libraries Pressbooks / Russell Leigh Sharman

Supports 'cinematic language' as a set of rules and conventions by which cinema communicates, built from shots, editing, camera movement, lighting, sound, and design, and the idea that filmmakers and audiences share and refine these conventions.
